segments.text: For transthrastic lung ultrasound, let's start out with a discussion of probe selection.
As a high frequency probe, the linear probe provides the greatest resolution of the plural line.
However, this comes with a penalty of greater attenuation and therefore poor resolution of deeper
structures. Therefore, if you're only interested in evaluating lung sliding, for example,
in ruling out pneumothorax, the linear probe is a reasonable choice. For more comprehensive
of lung ultrasound, however, we favor the phased array probe. The phased probe provides generally
adequate visualization of the plural line, but also generates higher resolution images of deeper
structures. In addition, the smaller probe footprint minimizes issues with rib shadowing,
especially in acquiring images from the lateral and posterior chest. Either the abdominal or lung
presets are both acceptable exam types. While the lung preset will enhance A and B line
artifacts, this can make imaging deeper structures like the plural space more challenging.
Therefore, we suggest the abdominal preset is selected, especially when imaging the
cost of a frenic angle. Various protocols exist for lung ultrasound, with many point-of-care
users employing a method that interrogates four to six regions of each hemithorax.
We'll describe the protocol used by the CCUS team in which images are acquired from four
zones on each hemithorax.
It's very important to ensure your images are labeled at the time of acquisition.
This is because unlike bedside echo, it can be next to impossible to determine the anatomic
location of unlabeled images at the time of reporting.
We'll discuss the naming convention generally used by the CCUS team.
The first zone to acquire images at is denoted R1 or L1 with letters R and L indicating laterality.
This can be obtained by placing the probe at the second intercostal space in the mid-clovicular line.
With the marker dot pointed towards the patient's head, the depth should be set at around 10 centimeters
but may need to be adjusted for patients of different body habitants with the aim being to visualize both the plural line
and to determine whether an A or B line pattern exists.
Excessive depth will make plural line assessment challenging and should be avoided.
The next point to image is zone 2, which should be labeled R2 or L2 when recording clips.
This is obtained by placing the probe at around the fourth or fifth intercostal space
at the anterior axillary line.
The starting depth is also around 10 centimeters.
A few optimization points when imaging zone 1 and zone 2.
Firstly, ensure your probe is static with respect to the chest wall, as movement of the probe
may confound assessment of lung slide.
In addition, to enhance the appearance of A and B lines, the probe should be held perpendicular
to the plural line.
If your image quality is low, slowly fan the probe towards or away from midline until the
plural line and A or B lines are clearly seen.
In addition, when sliding laterally on the chest wall, keep in mind that the probe will

frenic angle in the far field. 13 to 16 centimeters is a good place to start but
often needs to be adjusted based on body habitus. In patients with
consolidation and plural of fusion with a positive spine sign, the vertebral
bodies are a good internal landmark to determine depth. They should be the
deepest structure seen in the far field. Note however in patients with well

caudad or cephalad so that both the intravedonal solid organ, either the liver or the spleen,
and the lung are well visualized. The respective solid organ should occupy the right most third
to half of your image. If too much of your image is occupied by the spleen or liver,
